summary:
OrbitScope is an open web platform that detects moving and changing celestial objects in real infrared images captured by NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope. Users simply enter an object’s name or coordinates. The system retrieves images of the target region from the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive, removes zodiacal light and detector artifacts, aligns and overlays the images, and displays them as a time-sequenced blink animation.
The platform fully addresses the challenge requirements. It offers blink, difference, and motion-color modes, Gaia/CatWISE overlays, 0.75–5 µm spectra, light curves, URL-based sharing, and automated asteroid and proper-motion searches. All results are cross-checked against NASA JPL, ESA Gaia, and CatWISE catalogues. Using real data, we detected asteroid 626 Notburga with a positional difference of just 1.6″ from JPL predictions and measured WISE 0855’s proper motion at 8.20″/year, consistent with the catalogue value of 8.15″/year. The Planet X module statistically tests the Ninth Planet hypothesis using live JPL orbital data.
Why does this matter? SPHEREx generates hundreds of frames for each observed region. OrbitScope makes this vast dataset accessible without programming skills, enabling students, educators, and amateur astronomers to explore the universe. The platform uses no fabricated data, labels findings as candidates rather than discoveries, and provides open-source code.   tercume et azerbaycancaya
details:
What Does OrbitScope Do and How Does It Work?

OrbitScope is a web platform that detects moving and changing celestial objects in real infrared images captured by NASA's SPHEREx space telescope. Users simply enter an object's name (e.g., "Barnard's Star") or its coordinates. The system then follows six steps:

  1. Target Identification: Converts the object's name into coordinates using Gaia, SIMBAD, and CDS Sesame.
  2. Archive Search: Searches the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive for all SPHEREx frames covering the target location. New data releases are automatically incorporated.
  3. Data Retrieval: Downloads only small FITS cutouts surrounding the target, rather than entire images.
  4. Image Processing: Removes zodiacal light and bad pixels, aligns the frames to a common coordinate grid, and combines observations from each visit.
  5. Motion Detection: Searches for moving objects. For asteroids, a static sky template is subtracted and residual detections are linked along straight-line trajectories. For stars, the precise centroid is measured in each observation visit.
  6. Verification: Cross-checks every result against NASA JPL, ESA Gaia DR3, and CatWISE2020 catalogues. Objects that are not listed in existing catalogues but exhibit genuine motion are retained as new candidates.

Results are presented through blink animations, difference and motion-colour modes, spectra across the 0.75–5 µm range, light curves, and downloadable CSV and GIF files. Images from Canada's NEOSSat satellite are also used for independent verification. The Planet X section statistically examines the Ninth Planet hypothesis using the Rayleigh test applied to live JPL orbital data.

Real Results

  • Asteroid 626 Notburga: Detected with a positional difference of only 1.6″ from its JPL-predicted position.
  • WISE 0855: We measured a proper motion of 8.20″/year, compared with the catalogue value of 8.15″/year (7.6σ).
  • ε Indi B: Its spectrum revealed signatures associated with water, methane, and carbon monoxide (CO).
  • False detections: Zero false "new object" candidates were recorded in the tested fields.

Raspberry Pi 5 Station

The entire system—including the backend, website, and full-screen kiosk—runs on a single Raspberry Pi 5 device.

The Raspberry Pi creates its own Wi-Fi network. Users can connect using a smartphone or tablet by simply scanning a QR code. No additional software installation is required.

When there is no internet connection, previously downloaded real SPHEREx data can still be analysed locally. An internet connection is only required to retrieve new observation fields.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Makes large-scale astronomical data accessible to everyone, including students, teachers, and amateur astronomers, without requiring programming knowledge.
  • Enables interactive astronomy lessons in schools and rural communities with limited internet access through the Raspberry Pi station.
  • Supports citizen science: users can review candidates, label them as "real" or "artifact", and share measurements in CSV format.
  • Provides a bilingual interface in Azerbaijani and English.

Technologies and Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, httpx, SQLite.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Aladin Lite.
  • Data Services: NASA IRSA (TAP, SIA, IBE), NASA JPL (SBDB, Horizons, SB Ident), ESA Gaia, CDS, CADC.
  • Infrastructure: Docker, nginx, pytest (more than 100 tests).
  • Hardware: Raspberry Pi 5.

What Makes OrbitScope Innovative?

  1. A Modern Approach to a Historic Discovery Technique: We bring the classic blink-comparison method, historically used in the discovery of Pluto in 1930, into the era of modern space telescope observations.
  2. Innovative Use of SPHEREx's Variable Filters: By analysing dozens of exposures of the same location, we extract both spectral information and light curves.
  3. Independent NEOSSat Image Alignment: We independently position raw NEOSSat frames in the sky using Gaia reference stars.
  4. Interactive Planet X Analysis: We demonstrate in real time how sample selection can influence statistical conclusions about the Ninth Planet hypothesis.

Our Commitment to Scientific Integrity and Reliability

  • Scientific Integrity: No fabricated data is used. If an external service becomes unavailable, the system reports this transparently. Potential findings are labelled as "candidates", never as confirmed discoveries. Bright saturated stars are excluded from astrometric measurements.
  • Resilience: If NASA's primary service becomes unavailable, the system uses alternative access routes and cached data where possible.
  • Performance: Background processing, progress indicators, and caching make previously loaded observations available almost instantly when reopened.
  • Open Source: The source code is publicly available under the MIT License. Each result includes a shareable link and access to its original data file.

Learn about NEOSSat, the world's first space telescope dedicated to detecting and tracking asteroids, comets, satellites, and space debris. This CSA resource highlights how Canada is helping protect our understanding of near-Earth space by contributing to international efforts to identify and monitor objects that could pose risks to Earth or spacecraft.

The CADC provides access to a vast collection of astronomical observations from Canadian and international telescopes and space missions. Through this resource, participants can explore real scientific data used by astronomers to study stars, galaxies, exoplanets, asteroids, and other celestial objects.

This tutorial demonstrates how to use Python to visualize data from Canada's NEOSSat mission. Follow step-by-step instructions to access spacecraft observations, create visualizations, and explore data collected by Canada's space telescope.

This dataset contains observations collected by NEOSSat, Canada's Near-Earth Object Surveillance Satellite. The data supports the detection and tracking of asteroids, comets, satellites, and space debris. Explore real observations from Canada's space telescope and learn how objects are monitored in near-Earth space.
